Polemical

/puh-LEM-ih-kul/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Polemical means relating to a strong verbal or written attack on, or controversial argument against, someone's opinions or positions.

Polemical means relating to a strong verbal or written attack on, or controversial argument against, someone's opinions or positions. Critics dismissed the documentary as a polemical attack rather than a fair examination of the issue.

Worked Example

When the city proposed replacing the old library with a parking garage, a local historian published a furious open letter in the newspaper. She did not weigh both sides politely; she attacked the plan's supporters point by point, called their budget projections a fantasy, and dared the council to defend the demolition in public. Supporters of the garage fumed, preservationists cheered, and everyone agreed the letter was written to start a fight. It was a polemical piece from its first line to its last.

The historian's letter mounted a strong, controversial attack on the plan and on its supporters' arguments, which is what polemical means.

How Polemical Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

contentious

contentious: causing or likely to cause heated argument

combative

combative: eager to fight or argue

Antonyms

conciliatory

conciliatory: intended to soothe or make peace

evenhanded

evenhanded: fair and impartial to all sides

How Strong Is It? — critical → vitriolic → polemical

critical vs. polemical

critical vs. polemical: A critical review points out flaws while still weighing the evidence, while a polemical one sets out to demolish the opposing position altogether.

vitriolic vs. polemical

vitriolic vs. polemical: A polemical essay wages an aggressive argument against its target's ideas, but a vitriolic one turns to sheer bitterness, attacking with venom that outruns any argument.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — polem

Root — polem: from Greek polemos, war or battle

Suffix — -ic

Suffix — -ic: relating to

Suffix — -al

Suffix — -al: characteristic of, pertaining to

Put it together

Put it together: Polemical is built on the Greek root polemos, meaning 'war,' a root that survives in English almost nowhere outside this word's own family. A polemical essay wages a small war of words against its target. The suffix -al, meaning 'characteristic of,' stacks onto -ic to describe anything that has the nature of that verbal warfare.

Use the root in a new word: polemicist

Use the root in a new word: polemicist: A writer who makes a career of such verbal warfare is called a polemicist, from the same Greek polemos, 'war,' that gives polemical its fighting spirit.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal, academic/journalistic register

Polemical typically describes essays, pamphlets, speeches, books, and tones (a polemical op-ed, a polemical style). It marks writing or speech that attacks a position rather than weighing it fairly, and it sits at the opposite pole from equivocal language, which avoids taking any clear stand at all.
